G04_original_finding: 2020 individual civil judgment $179m and same-day bankruptcy; Uber exposure posed as question, not corporate judgment.
V1_English_paragraph: A former Google self-driving engineer faced a civil judgment of one hundred seventy-nine million dollars in March 2020. Anthony Levandowski filed for bankruptcy just hours later. This was not his criminal sentence, and it was not a verdict against Uber. The question was whether Uber might have to help pay.
V2_English_paragraph: In March 2020, former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski faced a civil judgment exceeding one hundred seventy-nine million dollars. Hours later, he filed for bankruptcy. Uber had agreed to buy his startup and signed a conditional indemnification agreement covering certain legal risks. The judgment was personal, not a verdict against Uber. Could that agreement make Uber help pay?

G04_original_finding: Chronology reverses investigation: 'So Uber brought in a forensic investigation' follows description of closing. Stroz hired between Feb term sheet and April approval, before Aug closing.
V1_English_paragraph: And that was the problem with a fast-moving acquisition. The transaction could close. The engineers could go to work. But facts about what they had taken, disclosed, or retained did not disappear just because the ownership of the startup changed. So Uber brought in a forensic investigation.
V2_English_paragraph: Before the acquisition closed, Uber had already hired forensic investigators to examine possible Google information retained by the engineers. The startup could be acquired and its staff could move jobs, but the questions surrounding their former employer's documents would not disappear. Those investigators would become central to the dispute.
G04_requested_fix: Replace close with: 'That was why Uber had already hired forensic investigators before the acquisition closed. Their findings would become part of the risk calculation.'

G04_original_finding: Too certain 'it would take a mistake ... to bring the conflict into the open'; prior dispute existed and email was a trigger, not sole necessary cause.
V1_English_paragraph: There was no tidy answer. Otto was acquired. Levandowski took a senior role in Uber's autonomous-driving work. And the eventual evidence dispute would not be settled by what one investigation did—or did not—find. It would take a mistake outside both companies to bring the conflict into the open.
V2_English_paragraph: There was no tidy answer. Uber completed the Otto acquisition, and Levandowski took a senior role in its self-driving program. Months after the deal closed, a supplier accidentally sent Google an email intended for Uber. It gave Google a new reason to investigate what its former engineer and Uber were building.
G04_requested_fix: Change to 'Then a supplier sent a LiDAR drawing intended for Uber to Google, giving Google a new reason to investigate.'

G04_original_finding: Similar-looking drawings phrased as objective resemblance, although Delaware opinion says allegedly resembled Google's drawings.
V1_English_paragraph: In December 2016, a supplier's email containing LiDAR-related drawings intended for Uber reached Google instead. It was the kind of accidental disclosure that can change how a company views its competitor's work. Similar-looking engineering material was suddenly in front of people who knew Google's own designs.
V2_English_paragraph: In December 2016, a supplier accidentally sent Google an email meant for Uber, containing circuit-board drawings for autonomous-vehicle technology. According to the later court account, the drawings allegedly resembled Google's own engineering designs. That alleged similarity raised questions about Uber's LiDAR work; the email alone did not prove that Uber had used Google's confidential files.
G04_requested_fix: State 'the attachments allegedly resembled Google's LiDAR designs', attributed to plaintiff/court summary.

G04_original_finding: Rhetorical phrase about unable to replay backup assumes absence of recoverable backups not determined; chronology of reported March2016 destruction implicit.
V1_English_paragraph: As the case moved toward trial, the record acquired another disturbing complication. Uber had disclosed information late about five computer disks that Levandowski was said to have destroyed. There were also questions involving electronic communications. The uncertainty about what had been on those disks could not simply be repaired by replaying a backup in court.
V2_English_paragraph: As the lawsuit moved toward trial, an earlier conversation acquired new significance. In March 2016, Levandowski told Uber executives that he possessed five disks containing Google information. According to Uber, he later reported destroying them, and Uber said it never received the disks. Uber's delayed disclosure to Waymo became an evidentiary dispute.
G04_requested_fix: Remove 'could not simply be repaired by replaying a backup'; state reported 2016 destruction and Uber's later disclosure to Waymo.

G04_original_finding: Says five disks 'destroyed during the Waymo–Uber dispute' even though reported destroyed shortly after Mar11 2016, before suit filed Feb2017. The January 2018 event is the PRETRIAL ORDER.
V1_English_paragraph: In January 2018, a federal judge addressed five computer disks reportedly destroyed during the Waymo–Uber dispute. He said jurors could draw an unfavorable inference from late disclosures—but they did not have to. The contents of the disks were not established by that ruling, and the case settled before any jury verdict.
V2_English_paragraph: In January 2018, a judge reviewed Uber's late disclosure that Anthony Levandowski had reportedly destroyed five disks after telling Uber about them in March 2016. He said jurors could draw an unfavorable inference, but were not required to. Uber said it never received the disks; their contents remained unverified. The case settled before a verdict.
G04_requested_fix: Replace paragraph and Short S05: 'In January 2018, a judge in Waymo’s lawsuit reviewed Uber’s late disclosure that Levandowski had reportedly destroyed five Google-related disks back in 2016. Jurors could, but did not have to, draw an unfavorable inference. The contents were not established, and the case settled before a verdict.'

G04_original_finding: 'Levandowski wanted to know whether' narrates internal mind-state; court records establish he later argued Uber should indemnify.
V1_English_paragraph: The judgment and bankruptcy were a financial crisis for Levandowski. But they exposed another question, one that reached straight back to the Otto acquisition. In April 2016, when Uber agreed to buy the startup, it had made a separate arrangement concerning certain legal liabilities. Levandowski wanted to know whether that agreement covered his enormous judgment.
V2_English_paragraph: The judgment and bankruptcy created a major financial problem for Levandowski. But an April 2016 indemnification agreement linked to Uber's Otto acquisition was still in dispute. Levandowski later argued that the agreement required Uber to cover the judgment. Uber disagreed about the scope of that protection, setting up a separate legal fight.
G04_requested_fix: Replace with 'Levandowski later argued that the 2016 agreement required Uber to cover the judgment.'
